paragraphs: 233 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in protein ubiquitination (GO:0016567).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, Casitas B‑lineage lymphoma‑b (CBLB), cytokine inducible a non-intersection pathway component-containing protein (CISH), and copper metabolism domain containing 1 (COMMD1) illustrate how ubiquitin-based signaling control is represented in the rheumatoid arthritis module. CBLB is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets components of antigen receptor signaling for ubiquitin-dependent modification, thereby modulating activation thresholds in lymphocytes; its inclusion in the enriched rheumatoid arthritis set indicates that ubiquitin-mediated control of adaptive immune activation is a feature of the disease-related network. CISH is a a non-intersection pathway component family protein that recruits ubiquitin ligase machinery to cytokine receptors and associated kinases, coupling cytokine signaling to receptor down-modulation, while COMMD1 modulates NF-κB signaling in part through effects on ubiquitin-regulated complexes; their enrichment suggests that ubiquitin-dependent tuning of cytokine and NF-κB pathways is embedded within the rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteome.

Cullin 1 (CUL1), cullin 3 (CUL3), and β-transducin repeat containing E3 ubiquitin protein ligase (BTRC) exemplify cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase architecture within the enriched proteins. CUL1 serves as a scaffold for Skp1–cullin–F-box (a non-intersection pathway component) complexes that catalyze polyubiquitination of phosphorylated signaling and cell cycle regulators, while CUL3 forms related complexes with a non-intersection pathway component-domain adaptors; their presence in the rheumatoid arthritis gene set points to broad cullin-dependent ubiquitin ligase activity in pathways selected by the disease. BTRC is an F-box substrate receptor that binds phosphorylated targets and presents them to CUL1-based a non-intersection pathway component ligases for ubiquitination, further supporting the prominence of a non-intersection pathway component-type E3 complexes among proteins linked to rheumatoid arthritis.

The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (a non-intersection pathway component/C) components anaphase promoting complex subunit 2 (ANAPC2), cell division cycle 20 (CDC20), and cell division cycle 27 (CDC27) demonstrate representation of cell cycle–directed ubiquitination. ANAPC2 is a core a non-intersection pathway component/C subunit that, together with other anaphase-promoting complex proteins, forms the catalytic ubiquitin ligase scaffold, whereas CDC27 is a tetratricopeptide repeat subunit that recruits co-activators and substrates. CDC20 acts as a co-activator and substrate adaptor that directs a non-intersection pathway component/C to key mitotic regulators; the enrichment of these subunits in the rheumatoid arthritis protein set indicates that ubiquitin-dependent control of cell cycle transitions, relevant to proliferating synovial and immune cells, is a recurrent feature of the disease-associated network.

F-box and cyclin family member 3 (FBXL3), F-box and cyclin family member 5 (FBXL5), and cyclin F (CCNF) highlight the contribution of F-box substrate receptors to the enriched pathway. FBXL3 and FBXL5 are leucine-rich repeat F-box proteins that act as substrate adapters in distinct a non-intersection pathway component ligases, conferring specificity toward phosphorylated targets involved in cellular homeostasis and stress responses. CCNF is an F-box protein that also carries a cyclin domain and assembles into a non-intersection pathway component complexes to ubiquitylate cell cycle regulators; their presence in the rheumatoid arthritis-associated set underscores the importance of combinatorial F-box–dependent substrate recognition within the broader ubiquitination landscape implicated in the disease.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term can be organized into several functional clusters that together elaborate the ubiquitination machinery represented in rheumatoid arthritis. A large a non-intersection pathway component/C–cell cycle cluster includes additional anaphase-promoting complex subunits (ANAPC1, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13) together with other cell division cycle components (CDC16, CDC23, CDC26, CDC34), which cooperate to ubiquitinate mitotic regulators and thereby coordinate cell cycle progression in dividing synovial and immune cells. A cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase adaptor cluster comprises other cullin scaffolds (CUL2, CUL5, CUL7), elongin complex components (ELOB, ELOC), a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component adaptors (BTBD1, DCAF1), and the neddylation regulator DCUN1D1, collectively supporting assembly and activation of diverse cullin-based E3 ligases. An immune- and receptor-proximal E3 ligase/adaptor cluster includes AREL1, ARIH2, CBLL2, DTX3L, DZIP3, and the extensive ankyrin repeat and a non-intersection pathway component box (a non-intersection pathway component) family (ASB1, ASB2, ASB4–ASB9, ASB10–ASB18), all of which recruit specific substrates to ubiquitin ligase cores and thus fine-tune signaling receptors and downstream mediators relevant to inflammatory pathways. Finally, a regulatory scaffold and quality-control cluster containing CAND1, COMMD1, and DET1 reflects proteins that modulate the assembly, exchange, or activity of ubiquitin ligase complexes and link ubiquitination to protein stability and transcriptional responses, indicating that multiple layers of ubiquitin system regulation are captured within the rheumatoid arthritis module.

Together, enrichment of the rheumatoid arthritis protein set for the protein ubiquitination pathway indicates that disease-related processes are strongly shaped by enzymes and adaptors that write and interpret ubiquitin signals. Within this network, CBLB, CUL1, and ANAPC2 stand out as drivers of the association because they represent central E3 ubiquitin ligase platforms for antigen receptor signaling, cullin–a non-intersection pathway component signaling hubs, and a non-intersection pathway component/C-mediated cell cycle control, respectively. The data imply that coordinated ubiquitination of signaling and cell cycle regulators is a recurring theme in rheumatoid arthritis pathophysiology, acting across lymphocytes, myeloid cells, and synovial fibroblasts. This is reinforced by well-characterized physical and functional interactions among the enriched proteins, such as the assembly of CUL1 with BTRC or a non-intersection pathway component substrate receptors into a non-intersection pathway component ligases and the cooperative action of ANAPC2 with CDC20 and CDC27 in the a non-intersection pathway component/C, which together exemplify how multi-subunit ubiquitin ligase complexes underlie the observed pathway enrichment in rheumatoid arthritis.

pathways.pathway_description: A protein ubiquitination process in which a polymer of ubiquitin, formed by linkages between lysine residues at position 48 of the ubiquitin monomers, is added to a protein. K48-linked ubiquitination targets the substrate protein for degradation. [GOC:cvs, PMID:15556404]
pathways.cell_context: Not resolved from the supplied pathway-level evidence.
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: K48-linked ubiquitination targets proteins for proteasomal degradation, a central mechanism for terminating signaling and controlling protein abundance; in RA, altered K48 chains could dysregulate inflammatory signaling, antigen presentation, and cell survival. Perturbation of this pathway may sustain NF-κB and MAPK activation or impair resolution of Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling, thereby promoting chronic synovitis.
Intersection-gene interpretation: ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, and ANAPC13 form the APC/C E3 ligase, which generates K48-linked ubiquitin chains on mitotic regulators and other substrates, linking cell-cycle–coupled proteasomal degradation to RA. Their enrichment suggests that RA involves altered K48-dependent turnover of APC/C substrates, potentially affecting proliferation and activation thresholds of synovial and immune cells.
PubMed literature synthesis: The RNF13 study shows that E3 ligase–mediated ubiquitination controls TLR receptor fate and lysosomal/proteasomal degradation, illustrating how K48-linked ubiquitination shapes innate immune signaling relevant to RA. The TRIM16 and TPL-2 papers further connect E3 ligases and ubiquitin-dependent control of MAPK and ferroptosis pathways to RA pathogenesis, supporting a model in which K48-linked ubiquitination broadly tunes inflammatory and cell-death responses in the disease.
Cell/tissue context: Evidence supports roles in innate immune cells (e.g., TLR-expressing myeloid cells) and synovial fibroblast-like cells in RA, with additional relevance to other activated immune cell subsets where MAPK and ferroptosis pathways are regulated. paragraphs: 58 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in protein a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination (GO:0070936).

Among the E3 ubiquitin ligases enriched in this term, TRIM21 is particularly notable in rheumatoid arthritis as an autoantigenic a non-intersection pathway component-type E3 ligase that catalyzes a non-intersection pathway component-linked polyubiquitin chains on immune substrates, thereby linking ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation to autoantibody responses and inflammatory signaling in the joint. SKP2, the F‑box component of an a non-intersection pathway component-type cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase, promotes a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination of cell‑cycle regulators and has been implicated in driving synovial fibroblast proliferation and survival, suggesting that aberrant a non-intersection pathway component–SKP2 activity may couple this pathway to pannus formation and joint destruction.

NEDD4L, a a non-intersection pathway component-domain E3 ligase, catalyzes a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination of membrane and signaling proteins and has been reported to modulate T‑cell and cytokine signaling pathways that are dysregulated in rheumatoid arthritis, indicating that altered NEDD4L-mediated ubiquitin turnover may contribute to defective immune homeostasis. HUWE1, another large a non-intersection pathway component E3 ligase, targets transcription factors and DNA damage regulators for a non-intersection pathway component-linked degradation and has been linked to inflammatory and stress-response pathways relevant to synovial tissue remodeling, while PRKN, a a non-intersection pathway component-type ligase mediating a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination of damaged mitochondrial proteins, provides a connection between mitochondrial quality control and inflammatory joint pathology through its influence on oxidative stress and cell survival in immune and stromal cells.

Within the cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase machinery, CUL1 and CUL3 scaffold distinct a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitin ligase complexes that control the stability of signaling intermediates and cell‑cycle regulators in synovial and immune cells, positioning them as central integrators of proteasomal degradation in rheumatoid arthritis. RBX1, the shared a non-intersection pathway component-box component, and CDC34, a a non-intersection pathway component chain‑extending E2 conjugating enzyme, cooperate with CUL1-based a non-intersection pathway component complexes to build a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitin chains on substrates, indicating that coordinated dysregulation of these components could amplify proteasome-dependent turnover of key inflammatory and proliferative regulators in the disease.

Another prominent group of proteins enriched in this pathway comprises the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13, CDC16, CDC23, CDC26, CDC27), a multi-subunit E3 ligase that generates a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitin chains on cell-cycle substrates to control mitotic progression and exit. Together with the mitotic E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2C, these proteins support high-throughput a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination of cyclins and related regulators, suggesting that altered a non-intersection pathway component/C activity in proliferating synovial fibroblasts and infiltrating immune cells could contribute to the hyperplastic and invasive character of rheumatoid pannus tissue.

The remaining proteins enriched in protein a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination can be organized into several functional clusters. A core “E2 conjugating enzyme” cluster (UBE2A, UBE2B, UBE2D1, UBE2D2, UBE2D3, UBE2D4, UBE2E1, UBE2E2, UBE2E3, UBE2G1, UBE2G2, UBE2H, UBE2K, UBE2Q2, UBE2R2, UBE3A, UBE3C) comprises enzymes that accept activated ubiquitin and cooperate with multiple E3 ligases to assemble a non-intersection pathway component-linked chains on diverse substrates. A “cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase adaptor” cluster (SKP1, FBXO7, FBXO9, KBTBD6, KBTBD7, KLHL3, SPSB3, BTRC) contains substrate-recognition subunits that recruit specific targets to CUL1- or CUL3-based ligases for a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination. A “a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component E3 ligase” cluster (ARIH2, DTX3L, HACE1, RNF115, RNF126, RNF34, RNF4, RNF6, ZNRF1, ZNRF2, UBR4) encompasses ligases that tag signaling molecules, transcriptional regulators and damaged proteins for proteasomal degradation. Finally, a “regulatory and scaffolding” cluster (a non-intersection pathway component-related subunits as a functional module, together with RBX1 and CDC34 already discussed) reflects multiprotein assemblies that integrate these enzymes into higher-order a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination machines in rheumatoid arthritis–relevant cell types.

Overall, enrichment of protein a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitination (GO:0070936) indicates that rheumatoid arthritis risk and effector proteins are concentrated in the enzymatic systems that mark substrates for proteasomal degradation, thereby linking genetic susceptibility to dysregulated turnover of cell-cycle, signaling and stress-response regulators in the joint. The association appears to be driven in particular by TRIM21, SKP2 and NEDD4L, which connect a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitin signaling to autoantibody formation, synovial hyperplasia and immune dysregulation. Well-characterized interactions such as the assembly of SKP1–CUL1–RBX1–CDC34 a non-intersection pathway component complexes and the cooperation of a non-intersection pathway component/C subunits with UBE2C to ubiquitylate mitotic substrates exemplify how these proteins function together within this pathway. Collectively, these findings support a model in which perturbation of a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitin ligase and conjugating enzyme networks contributes to the chronic inflammatory and proliferative milieu that underpins rheumatoid arthritis pathology.

pathways.pathway_description: Any process that modulates the canonical NF-kappaB signaling cascade. [GOC:jl, PMID:12773372]
pathways.cell_context: Innate and adaptive immune cells in the rheumatoid synovium—especially macrophages, dendritic cells, and T cells—where ubiquitin-dependent regulation of canonical NF‑κB signaling drives pro‑inflammatory cytokine production.
pathways.disease_interpretation:
Disease pathology and relevance: Dysregulated canonical NF-κB signaling is central to RA, driving expression of cytokines, chemokines, and matrix-degrading enzymes in joint tissues. Modulation of this pathway can therefore influence both the intensity and persistence of synovial inflammation and joint destruction.
Intersection-gene interpretation: BTRC and FBXW11 encode F-box proteins that, together with CUL1, form SCF complexes targeting IκB for ubiquitination, thereby enabling NF-κB activation, while HUWE1 and CCDC22 participate in broader regulatory control of NF-κB pathway components. Altered expression or activity of these intersection genes could shift NF-κB signaling thresholds, affecting how cells respond to TNF, IL-1β, and other inflammatory cues in RA.
PubMed literature synthesis: The article "Opposing regulation of TNF responses by IFN-gamma and a PGE2-cAMP axis that is apparent in rheumatoid and immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced arthritis human IL-1beta+ macrophages" highlights context-dependent modulation of NF-κB–driven TNF responses in RA macrophages. "Cell-Type Targeted NF-kappaB Inhibition for the Treatment of Inflammatory Diseases" underscores the therapeutic importance of selectively dampening NF-κB in specific cell types, while "BAFF Promotes FLS Activation Through BAFFR-Mediated Non-canonical NF-kappaB Pathway and the Effects of CP-25" shows that NF-κB signaling (canonical and non-canonical) is a key driver of fibroblast-like synoviocyte activation in RA.
Cell/tissue context: Human IL-1β+ macrophages and fibroblast-like synoviocytes in the rheumatoid joint are directly supported by the attached literature. [PMID:40662950] [PMID:32640727] [PMID:36645607]

paragraphs: 14 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in regulation of canonical NF-kappaB signal transduction (GO:0043122).

Among the proteins listed for this record, UBE2N and its co-factor UBE2V1 form a well-characterized ubiquitin-conjugating complex that builds a non-intersection pathway component-linked polyubiquitin chains, a modification that promotes activation of canonical NF-kappaB signaling. In experimental models of inflammatory arthritis, UBE2N-dependent ubiquitination in myeloid cells is required for optimal pro-inflammatory cytokine production and maintenance of chronic synovial inflammation, consistent with the enrichment of UBE2N and UBE2V1 in this pathway and the central role of canonical NF-kappaB signaling in macrophage-driven disease. RBCK1 is a ubiquitin ligase that cooperates with a non-intersection pathway component-linked chain formation to assemble hybrid ubiquitin structures on signaling adaptors upstream of NF-kappaB, and genetic or functional disruption of RBCK1 impairs NF-kappaB–dependent cytokine expression and leads to immune dysregulation with inflammatory arthropathy; its presence in the enriched set therefore links ubiquitin-dependent NF-kappaB activation to joint-specific pathology.

BTRC, previously noted in this dataset, and its close paralogue FBXW11 are F-box substrate receptors that recognize phosphorylated inhibitors of NF-kappaB and target them for ubiquitin-dependent degradation, thereby permitting nuclear translocation of NF-kappaB transcription factors in the canonical pathway. Their enrichment in this term aligns with observations that persistent activation of canonical NF-kappaB in synovial macrophages and fibroblast-like synoviocytes sustains production of inflammatory mediators in rheumatoid arthritis, and that pharmacological strategies aimed at dampening NF-kappaB activity can ameliorate experimental arthritis. CUL1 and RBX1, which assemble with BTRC or FBXW11 into a non-intersection pathway component-type ubiquitin ligase complexes, are essential for this proteasomal control step; perturbation of a non-intersection pathway component complex function alters sensitivity of synovial and immune cells to pro-inflammatory stimuli, reinforcing the link between these core ubiquitination components and NF-kappaB–driven joint inflammation.

The remaining proteins enriched in regulation of canonical NF-kappaB signal transduction can be organized into three functional clusters. A first cluster of ubiquitin ligases and ligase-like adaptors—HUWE1, PRKN, TRIM32 and TRIM39—contributes to ubiquitin-dependent tuning of NF-kappaB signaling, with these enzymes modifying components of receptor-proximal or nuclear complexes that shape the intensity and duration of inflammatory transcriptional responses in joint-resident and infiltrating immune cells. A second cluster centers on signaling adaptors and scaffold-like molecules, including MIB2 and CCDC22, which participate in assembly or stability of receptor-associated complexes that couple extracellular inflammatory cues to canonical NF-kappaB activation, processes that are implicated in sustaining pro-inflammatory macrophage polarization and synovial stromal cell activation in rheumatoid arthritis. A third cluster consists of ubiquitin-like pathway components, exemplified by UFL1, which mediates conjugation of the ubiquitin-like modifier a non-intersection pathway component and has been linked to endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis and cellular stress responses that intersect with NF-kappaB signaling, thereby providing an additional layer of regulation over inflammatory gene expression in the arthritic joint.

Overall, enrichment of these 14 proteins in regulation of canonical NF-kappaB signal transduction underscores that rheumatoid arthritis risk and disease biology converge on ubiquitin-dependent control of this central inflammatory pathway in macrophages, synovial fibroblasts and lymphoid cells. Within this network, UBE2N, RBCK1 and BTRC appear to be key drivers of the association by directly modulating the ubiquitin scaffolds, ligase activities and inhibitor turnover that determine NF-kappaB activation thresholds. Well-documented interactions among the proteins listed for this record, such as the formation of a functional a non-intersection pathway component-linked ubiquitin-conjugating complex by UBE2N with UBE2V1, and the assembly of BTRC or FBXW11 together with CUL1 and RBX1 into a non-intersection pathway component ligase complexes, highlight how coordinated ubiquitination events fine-tune canonical NF-kappaB signaling in rheumatoid arthritis. These findings support the concept that therapeutically targeting discrete ubiquitin pathway nodes that regulate canonical NF-kappaB may provide cell type–selective strategies to attenuate chronic joint inflammation while preserving essential immune functions.

pathways.pathway_description: Any process that modulates the frequency, rate or extent of autophagy. Autophagy is the process in which cells digest parts of their own cytoplasm. [GOC:dph, GOC:tb]

paragraphs: 19 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in regulation of autophagy (GO:0010506).

Among the proteins listed for this record, TRIM21 stands out as a prototypical immune-regulatory E3 ubiquitin ligase that also modulates autophagy. TRIM21 is a well-established autoantigen in systemic autoimmunity and has been implicated in rheumatoid arthritis–related autoantibody responses, placing it at the interface of ubiquitin-dependent proteostasis, selective autophagy, and adaptive immune activation. Its ability to ubiquitinate antibody-bound targets links immune-complex handling to autophagic degradation, providing a plausible route by which dysregulated TRIM21 function could influence synovial antigen persistence and inflammatory tone in rheumatoid arthritis. KEAP1 is another central regulator of autophagy-relevant stress responses, functioning as a substrate adaptor in a ubiquitin ligase complex that targets redox-sensitive transcriptional regulators for degradation. In rheumatoid arthritis, where oxidative stress and synovial tissue damage are prominent, altered KEAP1 activity has been associated with impaired cytoprotective signaling and may secondarily modulate autophagy-dependent survival of synovial fibroblasts and macrophages, consistent with the broader literature highlighting redox-sensitive control of autophagy in this disease.

PRKN provides a direct mechanistic bridge between regulation of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control. As a ubiquitin ligase central to mitophagy, PRKN decorates damaged mitochondria with ubiquitin chains that recruit autophagy machinery, and mitophagy has been specifically highlighted in the attached literature as a contributor to bone metabolic alterations and inflammatory cell death in rheumatoid arthritis. In the context of rheumatoid arthritis, where mitochondrial dysfunction and altered energy metabolism have been reported in synovial cells and immune subsets, enrichment of PRKN in this pathway supports a model in which defective mitophagy can exacerbate both joint destruction and aberrant survival of inflammatory cells. VHL, another oxygen-sensitive ubiquitin ligase in the intersection, participates in the adaptation to hypoxia, a defining feature of the rheumatoid synovium; by targeting hypoxia-inducible transcriptional regulators for degradation, VHL indirectly shapes autophagy responses to low-oxygen stress and may influence pannus expansion and osteoclast activity in line with autophagy-related mechanisms discussed for bone metabolic disorders in rheumatoid arthritis.

The remaining proteins enriched in this term fall into several functional clusters that collectively emphasize ubiquitin-dependent control of autophagy. A first cluster comprises substrate-recognition components of cullin-a non-intersection pathway component and related ubiquitin ligase assemblies, including FBXL4, FBXO7, FBXW7, KLHL22, and LRSAM1, which provide specificity for ubiquitination of proteins that can serve as autophagy receptors, signaling adaptors, or metabolic regulators; through this, they help set thresholds for autophagosome initiation and cargo selection in cells exposed to chronic inflammatory cues. A second cluster consists of multifunctional E3 enzymes with established roles in protein quality control and turnover, such as HERC1, HUWE1, NEDD4, TRIM32, STUB1, RNF41, UBR4, and RBX1, whose activities converge on the proteasome–autophagy interface by tagging misfolded or damaged proteins, receptors, and signaling intermediates for degradation, thereby shaping the balance between survival and death pathways in rheumatoid arthritis–relevant cell types. A third, more specialized cluster is represented by UBE2A, an E2 conjugating enzyme that supplies activated ubiquitin to these ligases, and UFL1, which directs ufmylation, a ubiquitin-like modification implicated in endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis; together they underscore how multiple post-translational modification systems cooperate to fine-tune autophagic flux under the persistent cytokine, oxidative, and mechanical stress described in the rheumatoid joint.

Taken together, enrichment of these 19 proteins in “regulation of autophagy” suggests that ubiquitin- and ufmylation-dependent control of autophagy is a key organizational feature of the rheumatoid arthritis molecular network, spanning mitochondrial quality control, oxidative stress adaptation, hypoxia responses, and protein quality surveillance. TRIM21, KEAP1, and PRKN appear to drive the association by virtue of their well-characterized roles at the intersection of autophagy with autoimmunity, redox biology, and mitophagy, respectively, in settings that align with the autophagy-focused rheumatoid arthritis literature provided. Notably, RBX1 forms a ubiquitin ligase complex with KEAP1, and PRKN functionally cooperates with UBE2A, illustrating that several of the proteins listed for this record physically or functionally interact within shared ubiquitin ligase assemblies that modulate autophagic activity. These interconnected modules provide a coherent mechanistic framework in which perturbations of autophagy regulation can promote persistent inflammation, synovial hyperplasia, and abnormal bone remodeling in rheumatoid arthritis.

paragraphs: 161 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in ubiquitin-protein transferase activity (GO:0004842).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, CUL3, HUWE1 and HERC2 exemplify large, multifunctional ubiquitin ligases that are poised to integrate inflammatory and stress responses in rheumatoid arthritis. CUL3 serves as a scaffold for a non-intersection pathway component-domain adaptor proteins to form cullin-a non-intersection pathway component E3 complexes that catalyze ubiquitin transfer to a broad range of substrates, providing a structural basis for selective ubiquitination events that can modulate pathways such as autophagy and stress responses that are implicated in the attached rheumatoid arthritis literature. HUWE1 is a a non-intersection pathway component-domain ubiquitin ligase with intrinsic catalytic activity, capable of building ubiquitin chains on diverse targets; its enzymatic profile positions it to influence cell survival and differentiation programs relevant to synovial inflammation, although a specific rheumatoid arthritis substrate is not defined in the supplied evidence. HERC2, a giant a non-intersection pathway component-like E3 with a non-intersection pathway component repeats, similarly provides ubiquitin-protein transferase activity to multiple nuclear and cytoplasmic substrates, and its presence in this enriched set highlights the contribution of large modular ligases to the ubiquitin-dependent control of immune and stromal cell behavior in the disease context described by the attached studies.

The anaphase-promoting complex components ANAPC11, ANAPC4 and CDC23, together with the E2 enzyme CDC34, represent a second prominent group of ubiquitin-protein transferases within the intersection. ANAPC11 is the catalytic a non-intersection pathway component subunit of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, while ANAPC4 and CDC23 are core scaffold subunits that organize substrate recognition and catalysis, and CDC34 provides the cognate ubiquitin-conjugating activity for certain cullin-a non-intersection pathway component assemblies. Although the supplied literature does not delineate a direct rheumatoid arthritis phenotype for these specific subunits, their shared ubiquitin-protein transferase activity exemplifies how regulated proteolysis of cell-cycle and signaling proteins can intersect with inflammatory proliferative responses in the rheumatoid synovium.

A broad set of cullin-a non-intersection pathway component and substrate adaptor proteins further expands the ubiquitin-protein transferase landscape in this pathway. CUL2 and CUL5 form the scaffolds of additional cullin-a non-intersection pathway component ligases, while FBXW11, FBXW2, FBXW8, FBXO2, FBXO4, FBXO6, FBXO7, FBXO9, FBXO10, FBXO11, FBXO17, FBXO21, FBXO22, FBXO27, FBXO30, FBXL3, FBXL5, FBXL14, FBXL22, FBXO40, FBXO44 and KLHL9, KLHL13, KLHL20, KLHL21, KLHL42 supply F-box or a non-intersection pathway component/Kelch substrate adaptors that confer specificity to these complexes. In parallel, ASB1, ASB2, ASB4 and ASB12 function as a non-intersection pathway component-box adaptors that typically recruit substrates to cullin-based E3s, BTRC provides another F-box receptor component, and CBLB and CBLL2 contribute a non-intersection pathway component-type ubiquitin ligase activity often linked to receptor and signaling protein turnover. Together, these proteins define an extensive cullin-a non-intersection pathway component adaptor network that can, in principle, target regulators of autophagy, mitophagy, T cell differentiation, and inflammatory signaling, the very processes emphasized in the attached rheumatoid arthritis literature, even though the specific substrate–ligase pairs are not specified here.

a non-intersection pathway component- and a non-intersection pathway component-type ubiquitin ligases constitute another functionally coherent cluster within the enriched term. HACE1, HECTD1, HECTD2, HECTD3 and HECW2 are a non-intersection pathway component-domain E3 enzymes that directly catalyze ubiquitin transfer from E2 intermediates to substrates, enabling the assembly of distinct ubiquitin chain types that can signal for proteasomal degradation or non-proteolytic outcomes such as altered signaling complex assembly. ARIH2, LRSAM1 and LTN1 contribute a non-intersection pathway component- or a non-intersection pathway component-related ubiquitin-protein transferase activities implicated in quality control of misfolded or stalled translation products, aligning with the emphasis on mitophagy and stress adaptation in rheumatoid arthritis tissues from the attached work. The a non-intersection pathway component family members HERC1, HERC4, HERC5 and HERC6 further add large, modular a non-intersection pathway component-like ligases that may modify key immune and stromal proteins, while DTX3L, DZIP3, LMO7, LNX1, MEX3C and LRSAM1 provide additional E3 or E3-associated activities that can remodel signaling complexes, even though the rheumatoid arthritis–specific substrates of these enzymes are not detailed in the provided evidence.

Taken together, enrichment of ubiquitin-protein transferase activity (GO:0004842) indicates that rheumatoid arthritis risk and effector proteins are concentrated in enzymes catalyzing ubiquitin transfer, consistent with a central role for ubiquitin-dependent remodeling of autophagy, mitophagy, inflammatory signaling and cellular differentiation described in the attached literature. Within this network, HUWE1, CUL3 and HERC2 stand out as large, multifunctional ligases that likely drive much of the statistical association by virtue of their extensive substrate spectra and regulatory reach. The numerous cullin-a non-intersection pathway component, a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component ligases and their adaptors together suggest dense interaction patterns among the proteins listed for this record, particularly within multi-subunit complexes such as cullin-based E3s and the anaphase-promoting complex. Overall, the result supports a model in which perturbation of ubiquitin-protein transferase activity is a key organizing principle for how genetic and molecular perturbations converge on pathogenic pathways in rheumatoid arthritis.

paragraphs: 108 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in ubiquitin protein ligase activity (GO:0061630).

Among the proteins listed for this record, PRKN stands out as a key driver of the enrichment and a mechanistically compelling candidate in rheumatoid arthritis–related tissue damage. PRKN is a a non-intersection pathway component‑type E3 ubiquitin ligase that tags damaged mitochondrial proteins to initiate mitophagy, and experimental targeting of its signalling axis has been shown to induce mitophagy and ameliorate systemic inflammatory bone loss, a process highly relevant to the bone destruction and systemic skeletal fragility that accompany chronic inflammatory arthritis. In this context, enrichment of PRKN within the rheumatoid arthritis protein set suggests that dysregulated ubiquitin‑dependent mitochondrial quality control may intersect with inflammatory bone remodelling in disease.

CBLB is another a non-intersection pathway component‑type E3 ligase enriched in this term that is strongly implicated in autoimmune arthritis. Acting at proximal antigen receptor signalling complexes, CBLB ubiquitinates key signalling intermediates to dampen T and B cell activation thresholds, and genetic deficiency of CBLB in experimental models leads to loss of peripheral tolerance and the spontaneous development or exacerbation of arthritis. Within the present pathway, its inclusion reinforces the idea that altered ubiquitin ligase activity at immune receptor complexes contributes to synovial inflammation and autoantibody production in rheumatoid arthritis.

BTRC and FBXW11, two F‑box proteins that assemble with CUL3 and RBX1 into a non-intersection pathway component‑type ubiquitin ligase complexes, provide an additional mechanistic link between this enrichment and inflammatory signalling in rheumatoid arthritis. These ligases recognize phosphorylated substrates within NF‑κB and Wnt pathways and catalyse their ubiquitination, thereby shaping transcriptional programmes that control synoviocyte activation, osteoclast differentiation and cytokine production. Their joint enrichment, together with CUL3 and RBX1, indicates that a non-intersection pathway component‑dependent substrate selection and turnover are a prominent feature of the rheumatoid arthritis ubiquitin ligase landscape.

The remaining proteins listed for this record can be grouped into several functional clusters of ubiquitin ligases and adaptors. One cluster comprises Cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase components and substrate receptors (CUL3, RBX1, FBXL22, FBXO2, FBXO4, FBXO6, FBXO17, FBXO27, FBXO30, FBXO40, FBXO44 and FBXW11), which assemble modular a non-intersection pathway component‑like complexes that confer substrate specificity to ubiquitination in immune and stromal cells. A second cluster includes a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component‑like E3 ligases (HACE1, HECTD1, HECTD2, HECW2, NEDD4, NEDD4L, HERC2, HERC4, HERC5, HERC6 and HUWE1), enzymes that form ubiquitin thioester intermediates and often regulate inflammatory receptor turnover, DNA damage responses and interferon signalling. A third group consists of a non-intersection pathway component‑type E3 ligases and a non-intersection pathway component‑a non-intersection pathway component proteins (AREL1, ARIH2, DTX3L, DZIP3, LRSAM1, LTN1, MEX3C, MGRN1, MIB2, MKRN1, MYLIP, PJA1, PJA2, RBBP6, RCHY1, RLIM, RNF111, RNF114, RNF115, RNF123, RNF126, RNF130, RNF138, RNF14, RNF144B, RNF19A, RNF19B and RNF213), which target signalling intermediates, transcriptional regulators and misfolded proteins. Finally, the a non-intersection pathway component proteins (ASB1, ASB2 and ASB4), together with CBLB and CBLL2, form an adaptor cluster that links specific substrates to larger ubiquitin ligase assemblies, further diversifying the range of proteins subject to ubiquitin‑mediated control in rheumatoid arthritis tissues.

Taken together, the enrichment of ubiquitin protein ligase activity suggests that rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis involves coordinated changes in multiple classes of E3 ligases that regulate mitochondrial integrity, antigen receptor signalling and inflammatory transcriptional networks. PRKN and CBLB emerge as principal drivers of this association, connecting ubiquitin‑dependent mitophagy and lymphocyte tolerance, respectively, to inflammatory joint and bone pathology. Their presence alongside BTRC, FBXW11, CUL3 and RBX1 highlights an interconnected a non-intersection pathway component‑type ligase system that likely shares substrates and signalling pathways in synovial and immune cells. This convergence on ubiquitin ligase–mediated control of key inflammatory and tissue‑remodelling processes underscores the pathway as a central node in rheumatoid arthritis biology and a potential focus for therapeutic modulation.

paragraphs: 110 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in ubiquitin-like protein ligase activity (GO:0061659).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, the cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase components CUL3 and RBX1 exemplify how ubiquitin-like protein ligase activity intersects with inflammatory regulation in rheumatoid arthritis. CUL3 provides a neddylation-dependent scaffold for E3 ligase complexes, while RBX1 contributes the catalytic a non-intersection pathway component domain that transfers ubiquitin or ubiquitin-like modifiers to substrates. Dysregulated neddylation has been shown to enhance inflammatory responses in rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes, and CUL3–RBX1-type complexes are prototypical neddylation targets, placing these proteins at a plausible convergence between altered neddylation and the amplified synovial inflammation reported in the disease.

PRKN represents a second mechanistically coherent link between ubiquitin-like protein ligase activity and rheumatoid arthritis–relevant pathology. As a a non-intersection pathway component-between-a non-intersection pathway component E3 ligase, PRKN catalyzes the ubiquitin-like modification of outer mitochondrial membrane proteins during mitophagy, and has been implicated in a non-intersection pathway component–a non-intersection pathway component-driven mitophagy that ameliorates systemic inflammatory bone loss. Because pathological bone erosion is a central feature of rheumatoid arthritis, enrichment of PRKN in this pathway suggests that defective or compensatory mitophagy-mediated ubiquitin signaling may contribute to the balance between inflammatory damage and tissue remodeling in the rheumatoid joint microenvironment.

The broader intersection is dominated by additional E3 ubiquitin or ubiquitin-like ligase components that can be organized into functionally coherent clusters. A second cluster is formed by a non-intersection pathway component- and a non-intersection pathway component-related ligases such as HACE1, HECTD1, HECTD2, HECW2, HERC2, HERC4, HERC5, HERC6, HUWE1, MGRN1, NEDD4 and NEDD4L, which form thioester intermediates with ubiquitin-like modifiers before transferring them to substrates and are well placed to mediate the heightened post-translational signaling inferred from studies of a non-intersection pathway component and neddylation in rheumatoid arthritis. paragraphs: 28 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in ubiquitin conjugating enzyme activity (GO:0061631).

Among the enriched enzymes, CDC34, UBE2N and UBE2L3 exemplify the core ubiquitin-conjugating (E2) activity described by this term, forming transient thioester intermediates with ubiquitin and passing ubiquitin on to downstream acceptors in conjunction with specific ligase partners. The clinical observation that auranofin targets the ubiquitin-activating step and enhances ubiquitin trans‑thioesterification to E2 enzymes in rheumatoid arthritis provides direct evidence that the same catalytic step executed by CDC34, UBE2N and UBE2L3 is pharmacologically and pathogenically relevant in the disease. Together with reports that small-molecule inhibition of ubiquitin transfer to immune signaling adaptors ameliorates autoimmunity, these E2 enzymes position the enriched module squarely at a ubiquitin-dependent control point for inflammatory signaling in rheumatoid arthritis.

Independent evidence that conjugating enzymes can drive rheumatoid arthritis pathology comes from studies of a non-intersection pathway component-conjugating E2 components and related modifiers, where a a non-intersection pathway component E2 has been shown to promote proliferation and migration of fibroblast-like synoviocytes and broader a non-intersection pathway component pathway components have been implicated in disease. Although the proteins listed for this record act on ubiquitin rather than a non-intersection pathway component, their shared reliance on thioester-based conjugation chemistry places UBE2C, a non-intersection pathway component family members (UBE2D1–UBE2D4), and a non-intersection pathway component family members (UBE2E1–UBE2E3) in an analogous mechanistic class whose dysregulation is already linked to synovial hyperplasia and chronic inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis. In this context, the enrichment of these enzymes suggests that altered activity at the conjugation step, rather than at substrate recognition alone, may be an important contributor to the rheumatoid arthritis gene module.

The remaining enriched proteins fall into recognizable functional clusters of ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes. One cluster comprises endoplasmic reticulum–associated E2s, including UBE2J1, UBE2J2, UBE2G1 and UBE2G2, which collectively support ubiquitin transfer within membrane-proximal quality-control pathways and thereby influence the turnover of receptors and signaling components relevant to inflammation. A broader cluster contains general nuclear and cytosolic E2s—UBE2A, UBE2B, UBE2H, UBE2K, UBE2L6, UBE2O, UBE2Q1, UBE2Q2, UBE2R2, UBE2S, UBE2U, UBE2W and UBE2Z, together with UBE2C and the a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component families—that collectively furnish ubiquitin to diverse ligase complexes, maintaining the dynamic ubiquitin landscape on transcription factors, signaling intermediates and cell-cycle regulators implicated in autoimmunity.

Taken together, the enrichment of ubiquitin conjugating enzyme activity in this rheumatoid arthritis module indicates that the thioester-based transfer of ubiquitin, rather than only downstream substrate recognition, is a key biochemical bottleneck in the disease network. CDC34, UBE2N and UBE2L3 emerge as central drivers of this association by virtue of their canonical E2 activity at the same conjugation step that is pharmacologically targeted and experimentally linked to autoimmune modulation. The shared mechanism of all proteins listed for this record—sequential thioester exchange of ubiquitin between carrier cysteines—also underpins their interactions with common activating and ligase partners, reinforcing the idea that coordinated perturbation of this enzymatic tier can propagate through multiple ubiquitin-dependent pathways in rheumatoid arthritis.

paragraphs: 132 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in ubiquitin ligase complex (GO:0000151).

Within this term, several rheumatoid arthritis associated cullin scaffold proteins, including CUL1, CUL2 and CUL3, are enriched in multi-subunit ubiquitin ligase complexes in which they provide the central structural backbone for assembly of a non-intersection pathway component-type ubiquitin ligases. Their shared presence in these complexes, together with their inclusion in the rheumatoid arthritis input set, indicates that a substantial fraction of the disease-linked proteins act at the level of cullin-based ubiquitin ligase architecture rather than as isolated enzymes.

CUL5 and CUL7 are likewise enriched as cullin scaffolds, but they assemble distinct ubiquitin ligase complexes that rely on specific adaptors such as DCAF1 to recruit substrates. The appearance of multiple cullin family members in this pathway is consistent with the broader observation that cullin-dependent ubiquitin ligases, exemplified by a non-intersection pathway component-mediated regulation of glycolytic metabolism in fibroblast-like synoviocytes, can influence the behavior of rheumatoid arthritis synovial cells, even though a non-intersection pathway component itself is not in the present intersection.

Among adaptor subunits, the F-box proteins FBXO11 and FBXO31, together with the β-TrCP family member BTRC, are enriched as substrate-recognition modules that couple specific protein targets to CUL1-containing complexes. Their co-enrichment with cullin scaffolds and with the elongin components ELOB and ELOC underscores that many of the rheumatoid arthritis associated proteins in this term participate not only in ubiquitin ligase activity per se but in specifying which synovial or immune cell proteins are selected for ubiquitination, as implied by their inclusion in the disease-focused input list.

The term “ubiquitin ligase complex” is a cellular component annotation, and the proteins listed for this record are enriched in multi-subunit ubiquitin-protein ligase assemblies that reside primarily in the cytoplasm and nucleus rather than in a discrete anatomic lesion of the rheumatoid joint. Core structural constituents include ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11 and ANAPC13 within the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, together with CDC16, CDC23, CDC26 and CDC27 as additional scaffold subunits, while CDC20 and CCNF act more transiently as co-activators or substrate adaptors on this a non-intersection pathway component/C platform; ARIH2 and COMMD1 represent further examples of proteins that can transiently associate with ubiquitin ligase assemblies. This co-localization within ubiquitin ligase complexes should not be taken as evidence that all of these proteins contribute to rheumatoid arthritis through a single shared mechanism, but rather that many of the disease-linked proteins operate in the same class of subcellular complexes.

The remaining proteins can be organized into several functional clusters. First, a “cullin–neddylation and assembly” cluster comprises CUL2, CUL3, CUL5, CUL7, DCAF1, CAND1, DCUN1D1, DCUN1D2, DCUN1D4, DCUN1D5 and DET1, which collectively support the assembly, substrate loading and neddylation-dependent activation of cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ubiquitin ligase complexes. Second, an “a non-intersection pathway component a non-intersection pathway component-box adaptor” cluster includes ASB1, ASB2, ASB4, ASB9, ASB11 and ASB12, which function as substrate-recognition modules within elongin–cullin ubiquitin ligases. Third, an “F-box adaptor” cluster contains FBXL13, FBXL14, FBXL15, FBXL16, FBXL17, FBXL19, FBXL20, FBXL22, FBXL3, FBXL4, FBXL5, FBXL7, FBXO10, FBXO15, FBXO17, FBXO2, FBXO21, FBXO27, FBXO32, FBXO4 and FBXO44, which decorate cullin scaffolds with distinct substrate-binding capabilities. Finally, an “elongin complex” cluster comprising ELOB and ELOC provides the small adaptor dimer used by many a non-intersection pathway component and some cullin ligases, while COMMD1 contributes to additional multiprotein ubiquitin-related assemblies.

Overall, the enrichment of rheumatoid arthritis associated proteins in the ubiquitin ligase complex term suggests that a major fraction of the disease-linked proteome operates within, or in close association with, multi-subunit ubiquitin ligase assemblies rather than as solitary enzymes. The pattern is driven particularly by the concentration of cullin scaffolds such as CUL1, together with substrate adaptors including FBXO11 and a non-intersection pathway component/C co-regulators such as CDC20. Well-documented physical interactions among proteins in this intersection, for example the assembly of CUL2 and CUL5 with the elongin heterodimer ELOB–ELOC and with a non-intersection pathway component family adaptors, highlight that multiple rheumatoid arthritis associated proteins can coexist within the same ubiquitin ligase complexes. These findings indicate that perturbations in how ubiquitin ligase complexes are assembled and targeted may be a recurrent feature of the molecular environment in rheumatoid arthritis tissues, even though this cellular component enrichment alone does not specify the direction or consequence of those perturbations.

paragraphs: 17 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in anaphase-promoting complex (GO:0005680).

Among the proteins enriched in this term, CDC20, FZR1 and UBE2C stand out because they are key mediators of anaphase-promoting complex (a non-intersection pathway component) activity and therefore have particular relevance for proliferative responses in rheumatoid arthritis tissues. CDC20 and FZR1 function as substrate-specifying co-regulators that transiently bind the a non-intersection pathway component and direct it toward distinct sets of mitotic targets, and their presence in the rheumatoid arthritis–derived module suggests that regulated entry into and exit from mitosis is an important feature of the cellular populations sampled here. UBE2C provides E2 ubiquitin–conjugating activity to the a non-intersection pathway component, supporting the multi-ubiquitin modification of mitotic substrates; its enrichment in this complex in the rheumatoid arthritis context indicates that the dataset captures not only the structural core of the complex but also the catalytic machinery needed to drive a non-intersection pathway component-dependent proteolysis.

CUL7, UBE2S and CDC27 further refine the picture of how a non-intersection pathway component-related ubiquitination capacity is represented in the rheumatoid arthritis module. CUL7 is a cullin family scaffold that participates in the assembly of multi-subunit ubiquitin ligase complexes and, when enriched together with canonical a non-intersection pathway component components, points to a broader capacity for cullin-based ubiquitin signaling within the same cellular compartments in rheumatoid arthritis. UBE2S acts as a chain-elongating E2 that extends ubiquitin chains on a non-intersection pathway component substrates after initial priming, complementing UBE2C and reinforcing that the rheumatoid arthritis module contains a nearly complete ubiquitin-conjugation apparatus around the a non-intersection pathway component. CDC27, a tetratricopeptide repeat–containing a non-intersection pathway component subunit, contributes to substrate recognition and co-activator binding; its inclusion underscores that the rheumatoid arthritis–enriched proteins are not limited to accessory enzymes but also incorporate integral architectural elements of the complex.

The remaining proteins can be organized into functional clusters within the a non-intersection pathway component localization. A first cluster comprises the core a non-intersection pathway component scaffold subunits ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11 and ANAPC13, which form the stable structural framework of the complex and together define the subcellular compartment captured by this GO:CC term; these are best interpreted as structural constituents rather than dynamic regulators in the rheumatoid arthritis samples. A second cluster consists of the tetratricopeptide repeat–rich subunits CDC16, CDC23 and CDC26, which cooperate with CDC27 to form extended binding platforms for co-activators and substrates and therefore shape the interaction surface of the a non-intersection pathway component without themselves conferring catalytic activity. A third, more auxiliary cluster is represented by CUL7 and UBE2S, which participate in ubiquitin ligase assemblies and ubiquitin chain extension, respectively, and should be considered transient or conditional residents of the a non-intersection pathway component-containing compartment rather than immutable structural elements. Collectively, these clusters emphasize that the GO:0005680 enrichment reflects co-localization within a multi-subunit ubiquitin ligase complex, and co-localization alone should not be taken as evidence that all of these proteins act through a single, unified disease mechanism in rheumatoid arthritis.

Taken together, enrichment of the anaphase-promoting complex cellular component term indicates that many proteins in the rheumatoid arthritis–associated module reside in, or transiently interact with, the a non-intersection pathway component, highlighting a prominent role for a non-intersection pathway component-containing compartments in the proliferative and differentiative states sampled in this disease. Within this framework, CDC20, FZR1 and UBE2C appear to drive the association by anchoring catalytic a non-intersection pathway component activity and substrate selection to the rheumatoid arthritis module, while the a non-intersection pathway component core subunits and tetratricopeptide repeat proteins provide the structural context for these regulators. Well-documented physical interactions between CDC20 or FZR1 and the core a non-intersection pathway component subunits, and between UBE2C and the a non-intersection pathway component during ubiquitin transfer, support the interpretation that these enriched proteins assemble into functional a non-intersection pathway component complexes rather than representing isolated components. Nonetheless, because GO:CC terms describe shared localization rather than function, these findings should be interpreted as evidence of compartmental co-enrichment in rheumatoid arthritis, not as definitive proof that all listed proteins participate in a single a non-intersection pathway component-dependent pathogenic pathway.

paragraphs: 41 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in a non-intersection pathway component ubiquitin ligase complex (GO:0019005).

The proteins listed for this record are annotated to co-localize within a non-intersection pathway component-type cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ubiquitin ligase complexes, which reside predominantly in the cytoplasm and nucleus and provide a platform for ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover. Within this compartment, core scaffold and adaptor components assemble with interchangeable substrate-recognition subunits and additional E3 ligases, so that some intersection proteins, such as CUL1, RBX1 and SKP1, act as structural constituents of the complex, whereas others, including the various F-box proteins and TRIM21, are more transient residents that cycle on and off specific a non-intersection pathway component assemblies. This enrichment therefore reflects shared localization within a multiprotein ubiquitin ligase complex rather than a single linear pathway, and co-localization alone is not evidence that all of these proteins act through a common disease mechanism in rheumatoid arthritis.

Among the notable a non-intersection pathway component components, TRIM21 stands out as a a non-intersection pathway component-type E3 ubiquitin ligase that also serves as a well-characterized autoantigen in rheumatoid arthritis, where autoantibodies against this protein are detected in a subset of patients and have been linked to systemic autoimmunity. In addition to its role in antibody-dependent cytosolic immune recognition, TRIM21 participates in ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, providing a potential mechanistic bridge between intracellular antibody sensing and proteasomal degradation pathways that are active in synovial inflammation. BTRC, an F-box protein that binds SKP1 and CUL1 to form a canonical a non-intersection pathway component complex, recognizes phosphorylated substrates involved in NF-κB signaling, positioning it within inflammatory cascades that are operative in rheumatoid arthritis synovium, even though its direct clinical association with disease susceptibility or severity is less clearly defined than that of TRIM21.

The catalytic core of the a non-intersection pathway component complex in this enriched set is represented by CUL1, RBX1 and SKP1, together with the F-box protein SKP2. CUL1 functions as a scaffold that bridges SKP1–F-box adaptor modules with the RBX1 a non-intersection pathway component domain protein, thereby organizing the active E3 ligase architecture on which multiple F-box receptors, such as FBXW11 or a non-intersection pathway component family members, can dock. SKP1 acts as the central adaptor linking CUL1 to numerous F-box proteins, while RBX1 recruits E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes to complete the ubiquitination machinery; SKP2, in turn, is an F-box protein that operates within this framework to target cell‑cycle regulators for degradation, consistent with the proliferative phenotype of fibroblast-like synoviocytes in rheumatoid arthritis, although a direct clinical association of SKP2 with the disease has not been firmly established.

The remaining proteins enriched in this cellular component term can be organized into functional clusters according to their roles in substrate recognition and auxiliary ubiquitin ligase activity. One cluster comprises a non-intersection pathway component-repeat F-box proteins (FBXW4, FBXW5, FBXW7, FBXW8, FBXW11), which act as substrate receptors for a non-intersection pathway component complexes, typically recognizing phosphorylated motifs on signaling and cell-cycle proteins. A second cluster encompasses leucine-rich repeat F-box proteins (FBXL3, FBXL4, FBXL5, FBXL7, FBXL13, FBXL14, FBXL15, FBXL16, FBXL17, FBXL19, FBXL20, FBXL22), which provide additional substrate specificity within a non-intersection pathway component assemblies and are implicated in diverse processes such as iron homeostasis and transcriptional control. A third group contains other F-box-only proteins (FBXO2, FBXO4, FBXO6, FBXO7, FBXO9, FBXO15, FBXO17, FBXO27, FBXO31, FBXO32, FBXO44), which serve as interchangeable receptors that recruit distinct substrates to CUL1–SKP1–RBX1 cores and thereby diversify ubiquitination outputs. Two additional cullin family members, CUL2 and CUL5, form related cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase cores that share a similar overall architecture with CUL1-based SCFs but use alternative adaptor systems, while the a non-intersection pathway component proteins (SPSB1, SPSB2, SPSB3, SPSB4) function as a non-intersection pathway component-box–containing adaptors for elongin-based ubiquitin ligase complexes that intersect functionally with a non-intersection pathway component-mediated pathways. Finally, CCNF, a cyclin-family F-box protein, and the E3 ligase a non-intersection pathway component-related proteins present in other pathways of this report collectively underscore the breadth of ubiquitin-dependent substrate recognition modules represented in this enriched compartment.

Together, these findings indicate that a substantial subset of the rheumatoid arthritis protein module is enriched in the a non-intersection pathway component ubiquitin ligase complex, highlighting a convergence of disease-associated proteins within cullin–a non-intersection pathway component–based ubiquitin machinery rather than pointing to a single shared signaling cascade. The association appears to be driven principally by core scaffold and adaptor components such as CUL1 and SKP1, along with the autoimmune E3 ligase TRIM21, which anchor many of the other F-box and accessory proteins within this compartment. Well-documented physical interactions between CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1, and their assembly with F-box proteins such as BTRC or a non-intersection pathway component family members, provide a structural framework through which these enriched proteins can participate in proteasome-targeting complexes in rheumatoid arthritis tissues. Nonetheless, because the enrichment is defined at the level of subcellular co-localization, additional functional studies are required to determine which specific a non-intersection pathway component assemblies and substrates are most relevant to rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis.

paragraphs: 95 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Ubiquitin mediated proteolysis (KEGG:04120).

Within this pathway, SOCS1 and SOCS3 stand out as substrate-recognition components of CUL5-based ubiquitin ligase complexes that limit cytokine and growth-factor signaling by targeting receptor–proximal signaling proteins for degradation. In rheumatoid arthritis, both proteins are reported to modulate inflammatory signaling in synovial tissue, and their enrichment here supports a model in which altered ubiquitin-dependent turnover of a cytokine-associated kinase–a cytokine-responsive transcription factor pathway intermediates contributes to persistent inflammatory activation of synovial macrophages and fibroblast-like synoviocytes.

KEAP1 and the a non-intersection pathway component proteins KLHL9 and KLHL13 function as CUL3 adaptors and position this enrichment squarely on the KEGG map segment that links ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis to redox-responsive transcription. KEAP1-mediated ubiquitination of a non-intersection pathway component connects this pathway to the oxidative stress axis highlighted in the low-protein diet study in K/BxN rheumatoid arthritis mice, implying that dysregulated CUL3–KEAP1 complexes may influence a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component/ROS homeostasis and thereby shape macrophage polarization in inflamed synovium.

The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome branch of the map is densely covered by ANAPC1, ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13 together with CDC16, CDC20, CDC23, CDC26 and CDC27, indicating strong enrichment at the level of a multisubunit E3 ligase that governs cell-cycle transitions through targeted proteolysis. SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1, together with F-box proteins such as BTRC, FBXW11, FBXW7, FBXW8, FBXO2 and FBXO4, populate the a non-intersection pathway component branch, which in the KEGG map connects ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis to adjacent cell cycle and NF-κB signaling pathways through regulated degradation of key transcriptional regulators and cell-cycle inhibitors in proliferating synovial cells.

The remainder of the intersection proteins cluster into several functional groups along the downstream ubiquitination machinery of the KEGG map. A first cluster comprises ubiquitin-activating and -conjugating enzymes (UBA1, UBA3, UBA6, UBA7 and UBE2A), marking the E1 and E2 tiers that feed ubiquitin to multiple E3 ligases. A second cluster includes cullin scaffold and adaptor components (CUL2, CUL3, CUL5, CUL7, RNF7, ELOB, ELOC, DET1 and SOCS1), which assemble distinct cullin–a non-intersection pathway component complexes that target diverse signaling substrates and provide crosstalk to adjacent KEGG pathways such as hypoxia and growth-factor signaling. A third cluster consists of a non-intersection pathway component and a non-intersection pathway component E3 ligases (HERC1, HERC2, HERC4, HUWE1, NEDD4, NEDD4L, SMURF1, SMURF2, STUB1, TRIM32, TRIM37, TRIP12, PRKN, MGRN1, RCHY1, SIAH1, CBLB and RNF7), several of which participate in a non-intersection pathway component-β, NF-κB and mitophagy maps by ubiquitinating receptor complexes, SMADs, or mitochondrial quality-control substrates. Finally, SKP2, FZR1, DET1 and the a non-intersection pathway component-associated F-box proteins (FBXO2, FBXO4, FBXW11, FBXW7, FBXW8) form a substrate-recognition cluster that determines pathway specificity by docking phosphorylated cell-cycle and signaling proteins onto a non-intersection pathway component or a non-intersection pathway component/C cores for degradation.

Together, these findings indicate that ubiquitin mediated proteolysis contributes to rheumatoid arthritis by concentrating disease-enriched proteins at the level of E1–E3 enzyme cascades and multi-subunit ligase complexes that govern inflammatory signaling, oxidative stress responses and synovial cell proliferation. SOCS3, KEAP1 and CUL1 appear to be key drivers of this association, linking cytokine signaling, redox regulation and a non-intersection pathway component-complex activity to the ubiquitin pathway enrichment. Well-documented interactions among these proteins, such as the assembly of CUL3–KEAP1 and CUL5–SOCS1/3 complexes and the a non-intersection pathway component complexes built on CUL1–SKP1–RBX1 with F-box adaptors including BTRC and FBXW11, suggest that coordinated alterations in these ubiquitin ligase networks may underlie a shared molecular axis across rheumatoid arthritis synovial pathobiology and related joint diseases described in the attached literature. The scattered yet pathway-focused distribution of hits across several contiguous E1/E2/E3 branches on the KEGG map also implies that modulation of specific ubiquitin ligase assemblies, rather than global ubiquitination, may represent a therapeutically tractable component of the rheumatoid arthritis proteome signature enriched in this pathway.

paragraphs: 251 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Antigen processing: Ubiquitination & Proteasome degradation (REAC:R-HSA-983168).

In the Reactome hierarchy, REAC:R-HSA-983168 is curated as a pathway-level antigen-processing event that sits under a broader parent event encompassing antigen processing by ubiquitination and proteasome-mediated degradation within the adaptive immune system. Among the proteins enriched in this term, CBLB is annotated as an E3 ubiquitin ligase that catalyses ubiquitin transfer to target substrates, functioning at a ubiquitination step that precedes their proteasomal degradation; in this pathway it acts as a catalytic component of a multiprotein complex rather than as a substrate. CBLL2, another a non-intersection pathway component-type E3 ligase, is likewise represented as a catalytic ubiquitin–protein transferase that operates in successive ubiquitination reactions within the same antigen-processing cascade, rather than in the identical reaction step as CBLB. Both enzymes, by modulating the ubiquitin tagging of intracellular proteins destined for degradation, contribute to the remodeling of antigenic peptides highlighted in the supplied literature on posttranslational antigen processing in autoimmunity, thereby offering a mechanistic link between ubiquitin-dependent antigen processing and rheumatoid arthritis–related antigen presentation, even though the cited work does not provide gene-specific rheumatoid arthritis data for these ligases.

CUL1, enriched in this pathway, is annotated as the central scaffold of a cullin–a non-intersection pathway component E3 ubiquitin ligase complex that catalyses polyubiquitination of protein substrates; within the Reactome event structure it provides a non-catalytic but essential structural platform that brings together the catalytic a non-intersection pathway component subunit and substrate adaptors, positioning it in the same ubiquitination reaction step as its associated adaptor modules. DCAF1 functions here as a substrate receptor for a distinct cullin-based ligase, serving as a non-catalytic component that confers substrate specificity to the ubiquitination machinery and acting in a successive step relative to CUL1-based complexes in the overall antigen-processing sequence. ATG7, in contrast, is an E1-like activating enzyme for ubiquitin-like modifiers in autophagy-related conjugation, catalysing the ATP-dependent activation and transfer of these modifiers; in the context of this antigen-processing pathway it is annotated as a catalyst that primes ubiquitin-like molecules, thereby feeding into downstream ubiquitination and degradation steps that shape the antigenic peptide repertoire relevant to rheumatoid arthritis–associated autoantigen generation as discussed in the literature on posttranslational antigen remodeling.

Further enriched proteins in this pathway cluster into several mechanistic modules. First, multiple subunits of the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (a non-intersection pathway component/C), including ANAPC2, ANAPC4, ANAPC5, ANAPC7, ANAPC10, ANAPC11, ANAPC13, CDC16, CDC20, CDC23, CDC26 and CDC27, together with the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme CDC34 and the F-box protein CCNF, are annotated as components (and, for CDC34, a catalytic E2) of large E3 ubiquitin ligase assemblies that catalyse the ubiquitination of cell cycle–regulated substrates; in this antigen-processing pathway they are represented as structural or catalytic elements of ubiquitination complexes that act across successive steps of substrate tagging, upstream of proteasomal degradation. Second, the a non-intersection pathway component-box family members ASB1, ASB2, ASB4, ASB5, ASB6, ASB7, ASB8, ASB9, ASB10, ASB11, ASB12, ASB13, ASB14, ASB15, ASB16, ASB17 and ASB18 are grouped as substrate-recognition adaptors within cullin-based E3 ligases, functioning as non-catalytic components that recruit specific protein substrates for ubiquitination; in the Reactome representation they operate in multiple parallel ubiquitination reactions that converge on proteasomal processing of modified antigens. Third, the BC-box and F-box adaptors BTBD1, BTBD6, FBXL12, FBXL13, FBXL14, FBXL15, FBXL16, FBXL18, FBXL19, FBXL20 and FBXL22, together with the Elongin complex components ELOB and ELOC and the cullin scaffolds CUL2, CUL3, CUL5 and CUL7, form a network of cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase modules in which the cullins act as non-catalytic scaffolds and the adaptors serve as substrate receptors; these complexes participate in distinct ubiquitination steps within the same overall antigen-processing route. Finally, AREL1, ARIH2, DTX3L, DZIP3 and DET1 are annotated as catalytic E3 ligases or ligase regulators, while AREL1 and ARIH2 in particular are involved in endoplasmic reticulum–associated degradation, the process emphasised in the supplied literature as contributing to immune regulation and autoimmunity; in this pathway they catalyse ubiquitin transfer to misfolded or selected proteins, feeding substrates into proteasomal degradation that ultimately generates peptides for antigen presentation in the rheumatoid arthritis setting.

Together, the enrichment of these proteins in “Antigen processing: Ubiquitination & Proteasome degradation” indicates that rheumatoid arthritis–associated gene products are concentrated in ubiquitin-dependent steps that determine which intracellular proteins are selected, modified and delivered to the proteasome for peptide generation. Within this framework, CBLB, CUL1 and ATG7 appear to drive the association by anchoring key catalytic and structural positions in the ubiquitination and ubiquitin-like activation cascades that precede antigenic peptide production. The supplied literature on endoplasmic reticulum–associated degradation and posttranslational antigen remodeling in autoimmunity supports a model in which such ubiquitination and degradation events reshape the antigen repertoire presented to the immune system in rheumatoid arthritis, although it does not single out individual proteins from the present list. paragraphs: 145 submitted rheumatoid arthritis-associated proteins were significantly enriched in Neddylation (REAC:R-HSA-8951664).

Within Reactome, Neddylation (R-HSA-8951664) is annotated as a pathway-level event nested under the parent event Post-translational protein modification (R-HSA-597592), comprising a series of reactions in which target proteins are conjugated with, and subsequently deconjugated from, NEDD8. Among the proteins enriched in this pathway, the cullin scaffold CUL1 functions primarily as a neddylation substrate and as a structural component of cullin–a non-intersection pathway component E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes; in this context it participates in the same reaction step as its activating NEDD8 E3 ligases during conjugation, and in successive steps with deneddylating complexes that reset the scaffold. CUL3 and CUL5 similarly act as substrates and structural cores for distinct cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases, entering the pathway at the conjugation step and persisting as central components of the assembled complexes that are regulated by repeated cycles of neddylation and deneddylation in rheumatoid arthritis associated cells enriched for this pathway.

The a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunit COPS5, enriched here, is a catalytic component of the deneddylase complex that removes NEDD8 from cullin scaffolds; together with other a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunits, it acts as a catalyst across reaction steps that follow cullin neddylation, thereby controlling the transition from active to inactive cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases. In the same pathway, CAND1 operates as a regulatory factor that binds unneddylated CUL1, CUL2 and CUL3, stabilizing a state competent for exchange of substrate adaptors; it acts in a reaction step that is temporally downstream of COPS5-mediated deneddylation and upstream of renewed neddylation, thus linking successive cycles of activation and inactivation of cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases in the rheumatoid arthritis associated protein set enriched in Neddylation.

The remaining enriched proteins in this pathway can be grouped into several functional clusters. A first cluster comprises additional cullin scaffolds CUL2, CUL3, CUL5 and CUL7, which function as neddylation substrates and core structural components of distinct cullin–a non-intersection pathway component E3 ligase complexes, entering the pathway at the conjugation step and persisting across downstream ubiquitination reactions. A second cluster contains substrate adaptor modules for these ligases, including the a non-intersection pathway component family members ASB1, ASB2, ASB4, ASB5, ASB6, ASB7, ASB8, ASB9, ASB10, ASB11, ASB12, ASB13, ASB14, ASB15, ASB16, ASB17 and ASB18, the a non-intersection pathway component/a non-intersection pathway component proteins BTBD1 and BTBD6, the F-box proteins FBXL12, FBXL13, FBXL14, FBXL15, FBXL16, FBXL18 and FBXL19, as well as CCNF, BTRC, CCDC22 and CISH; these proteins act mainly as components of multi-subunit cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase complexes and as neddylation-regulated substrates that assemble into the same reaction steps in which active ligase complexes are formed. A third cluster encompasses the a non-intersection pathway component signalosome structural subunits COPS2, COPS3, COPS4, COPS6, COPS7A, COPS7B and COPS8, which are non-catalytic components of the deneddylase complex that act together with COPS5 in the deneddylation step. A fourth cluster is formed by the a non-intersection pathway component family members DCUN1D1, DCUN1D2, DCUN1D4 and DCUN1D5, which function as NEDD8 E3 ligase components that catalyse cullin neddylation in reaction steps upstream of a non-intersection pathway component signalosome-mediated deneddylation. A fifth cluster includes ELOB and ELOC, which act as components of elongin-based substrate adaptor complexes for cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligases, and the a non-intersection pathway component proteins COMMD1, COMMD2, COMMD3, COMMD4, COMMD5, COMMD6, COMMD7, COMMD8, COMMD9 and COMMD10, which participate as adaptor or regulatory components within ubiquitin ligase-associated complexes, acting in the same assembly and substrate-recognition steps as the a non-intersection pathway component, a non-intersection pathway component and F-box proteins.

Overall, enrichment of rheumatoid arthritis associated proteins in the Neddylation pathway indicates that cyclic NEDD8 conjugation and removal on cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase complexes is a central post-translational mechanism modulating ubiquitin-dependent signalling in this disease. The association appears to be driven primarily by the cullin scaffold CUL1, the deneddylase subunit COPS5 and the cullin regulator CAND1, which together span successive steps from cullin activation through deneddylation and recycling. Consistent with prior evidence that dysregulated neddylation enhances inflammatory responses in rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes, the concerted presence of a non-intersection pathway component family ligases and a non-intersection pathway component signalosome components among the enriched proteins supports a model in which altered balance between neddylation and deneddylation perturbs cullin–a non-intersection pathway component ligase activity. Well-documented interactions within this pathway, such as those between CUL1 and CAND1 and between cullin scaffolds and the a non-intersection pathway component signalosome subunits including COPS5, highlight specific protein–protein interfaces through which neddylation-dependent control of inflammatory signalling may be disrupted in rheumatoid arthritis.
